panels.title: Logging rate
panels.description: Shows the rate of logging the messages by their level. Unexpected spike in rate is a good reason to check logs.

panels.title: RSS memory % usage ($instance)
panels.description:
How much resident memory (RAM) the process is actually using, compared to its allowed container or system limit.

- Good: Below 70% most of the time, maybe spiking a bit under load.
- Bad: Above 90% for more than 5 minutes = risk of out-of-memory (OOM) kill.

panels.title: RSS anonymous memory % usage ($instance)
panels.description:
Share for memory allocated by the process itself. When memory usage reaches 100% it will be likely OOM-killed.
Safe memory usage % considered to be below 80%

panels.title: CPU pressure
panels.description:
CPU pressure based on [Pressure Stall Information](https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html).

**Lower is better.**

Pressure is measured as amount of time within 1sec time window the process was:
- waiting: at least one task in the process was ready to run (runnable) but couldn't get scheduled on the CPU.
- stalled: all tasks in the process (except idle ones) were unable to get CPU time — a full CPU stall.

If there's a CPU burst, it's normal to see waiting or stalled > 100ms. It only becomes a concern if it consistently climbs above 50-100ms and aligns with latency spikes or GC slowdowns.

queries.query: sum(go_memstats_sys_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by (job) + sum(vm_cache_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by (job)

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: CPU cores used by instance

panels.title: Memory pressure
panels.description:
Shows memory pressure based on [Pressure Stall Information](https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html).

**Lower is better.**

Pressure is measured as amount of time within 1sec time window the process was:
- waiting: at least one thread was blocked on memory.
- stalled: every thread was blocked on memory (severe pressure).

Elevated memory pressure can slowdown the process performance by utilizing more disk IO. Consider increasing amount of available RAM limit or decreasing the load on the process.

See major page faults rate panel in Troubleshooting section if this metric continued to be high.

panels.title: Disk writes/reads ($instance)
panels.description: Shows the number of bytes read/write from the storage layer.

panels.title: Open FDs usage % ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the percentage of open file descriptors compared to the limit set in the OS.
Reaching the limit of open files can cause various issues and must be prevented.

See how to change limits here https://medium.com/@muhammadtriwibowo/set-permanently-ulimit-n-open-files-in-ubuntu-4d61064429a

panels.title: Disk write/read calls ($instance)
panels.description: Shows the number of read/write syscalls such as read, pread, write, pwrite.

panels.title: IO pressure
panels.description:
Shows IO pressure based on [Pressure Stall Information](https://docs.kernel.org/accounting/psi.html).

**Lower is better.**

Pressure is measured as amount of time within 1sec time window the process was:
- waiting: at least one runnable thread blocked on IO (disk, NVMe, network-storage) while others could still make progress.
- stalled: all non-idle threads simultaneously waiting on `I/O`.

If stalled > 0, consider increasing queue depth on NVMe, raising blk-mq budgets, or relaxing cgroup I/O limits.

panels.title: CPU spent on GC ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the percent of CPU spent on garbage collection.

If % is high, then CPU usage can be decreased by changing GOGC to higher values. Increasing GOGC value will increase memory usage, and decrease CPU usage.

Try searching for keyword `GOGC` at https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/troubleshooting/

panels.title: Memory allocations rate
panels.description: Shows the rate of allocations in memory. Sudden increase in allocations would mean increased pressure on Go Garbage Collector and can saturate CPU resources of the application.

panels.title: Go scheduling latency
panels.description:
Shows the time goroutines have spent in runnable state before actually running.

**Lower is better.**

High values or values exceeding the threshold is usually a sign of            insufficient CPU resources or CPU throttling. 

Verify that service has enough CPU resources. Otherwise, the service could work unreliably with delays in processing.

panels.title: Network usage
panels.description:
Shows network usage by VM:
* Writes show traffic sent to clients
* Reads show traffic received from clients

panels.title: Churn rate ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the rate and total number of new series created over last 24h.

High [churn rate](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/faq/#what-is-high-churn-rate) tightly connected with database performance and may result in unexpected OOM's or slow queries. It is recommended to always keep an eye on this metric to avoid unexpected [cardinality](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#cardinality) "explosions".

The higher churn rate is, the more resources required to handle it. Consider to keep the churn rate as low as possible.

Good references to read:
* https://www.robustperception.io/cardinality-is-key
* https://www.robustperception.io/using-tsdb-analyze-to-investigate-churn-and-cardinality

panels.title: Slow inserts %
panels.description:
The percentage of [slow inserts](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/faq/#what-is-a-slow-insert) compared to the total ingestion rate. 

The lower the better. 

In short, slow insert is a cache miss. There are following reasons for slow inserts to go up: 
* Ingestion of completely new, not seen before time series;
* Not enough memory to maintain big enough caches for the current workload.

If percentage remains high (>10%) during extended periods of time, then it is likely more RAM is needed for optimal handling of the current number of [active time series](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/faq/#what-is-an-active-time-series). 

See [this issue](https://github.com/VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaMetrics/issues/3976#issuecomment-1476883183) for details.

panels.title: Assisted merges
panels.description: Merge assist happens when storage can't keep up with merging parts. This is usually a sign of overload for storage.

panels.title: Slow queries rate
panels.description: Slow queries rate according to `search.logSlowQueryDuration` flag, which is `5s` by default.

panels.title: Cache miss ratio ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the percentage of missed cache requests by cache type

The lower the better.

Red color means that cache's memory usage is at least 95% of its limit. Green means it is below 95%. Gray means usage is unavailable.

If misses remain high for long time period and the cache is near its limit (colored red), then it is likely more memory is required for this level of workload. Cache's memory limit depends on memory available to VictoriaMetrics component, so increasing the memory limit will automatically increase cache capacity. 

If misses remain high for long time period and cache hasn't reached its limit (colored green), then it could be that workload is changing too frequently (high churn rate, unique read queries) or is inconsistent enough for caches to expire.

See more about [caches in VictoriaMetrics](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#cache-tuning).

queries.query:
max(
    (
        rate(vm_cache_misses_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])
        /
        rate(vm_cache_requests_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])
    )
    and
    (
        vm_cache_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}
        /
        (vm_cache_size_max_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} > 0)
        >= 0.95
    )
) by(type)

max(
    (
        rate(vm_cache_misses_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])
        /
        rate(vm_cache_requests_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__rate_interval])
    )
    and
    (
        vm_cache_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}
        /
        (vm_cache_size_max_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} > 0)
        < 0.95
    )
) by(type)

panels.title: Cache usage % by type
panels.description:
Shows the percentage of used cache size from the allowed size by type. 
Values close to 100% show the maximum potential utilization.
Values close to 0% show that cache is underutilized.

panels.title: Samples dropped for last 1h
Deduplication rate ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the rate of samples dropped by [deduplication](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#deduplication) and [downsampling](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#downsampling).

Downsampling works the same way as deduplication: it keeps the last sample per `interval` for each series. The difference is that it applies only to samples older than the configured `offset`. That is why samples dropped by downsampling are counted here too.

Should be empty if neither `-dedup.minScrapeInterval` nor `-downsampling.period` is set.

Samples are dropped in two places:
* `type="merge"` - during [background merges](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#storage). Dropped samples are permanently removed from disk.
* `type="select"` - during [read queries](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#query-data). Samples are dropped only from query results, stored data is not changed.

When historical data has to be re-processed, for example after `-downsampling.period` or `-dedup.minScrapeInterval` is enabled or increased, partitions are re-merged in background. vmstorage checks for such partitions every `-storage.finalDedupScheduleCheckInterval` (1h by default). While these partitions are re-merged, the `merge` rate can be orders of magnitude higher than usual. This is expected and lasts until all matching partitions are processed.

The more samples need to be dropped, the higher will be resource usage.

panels.title: Non-default flags
panels.description: Flags explicitly set to non-default values

queries.query: sum(flag{is_set="true", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance, name, value)

panels.title: Restarts ($job)
panels.description: Shows the number of restarts per job. The chart can be useful to identify periodic process restarts and correlate them with potential issues or anomalies. Normally, processes shouldn't restart unless restart was inited by user. The reason of restarts should be figured out by checking the logs of each specific service.

panels.title: Major page faults rate
panels.description:
Major page faults occur when required data is not in physical memory and must be loaded from disk (storage or swap). It usually happens with:
- insufficient physical memory
- active use of swap space
- file mapping access

It may cause significant performance slowdown if sustained high.

Possible workaround:
- Extend RAM to scale up
- Reduce swap usage by adjusting vm.swappiness

panels.title: Fsync avg duration ($instance)
panels.description:
Average duration of fsync system calls. Spikes or high latency indicates that storage I/O cannot keep up with the write rate, which may slow down data ingestion.

If this value is elevated:
- Check disk-related metrics.
- If using cloud storage, check IOPS and throughput limits.
- If using NFS, check network performance, server resource usage, and any errors on the NFS server side.
- Check for known bugs in the filesystem or kernel version being used.

panels.title: Datapoints ingestion rate ($instance)
panels.description: How many datapoints are inserted into storage per second

panels.title: Storage full ETA ($instance)

queries.query:
(vm_free_disk_space_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}-vm_free_disk_space_limit_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) 
/ 
ignoring(path) (
    (rate(vm_rows_added_to_storage_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[1d]) - 
        sum(rate(vm_deduplicated_samples_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[1d])) without(type)) * 
    (
        sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type!~"indexdb.*"}) without(type) /
        sum(vm_rows{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type!~"indexdb.*"}) without(type)
    )
    +
    rate(vm_new_timeseries_created_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[1d]) * 
    (
        sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type="indexdb/file"}) without(type) /
        sum(vm_rows{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type="indexdb/file"}) without(type)
    )
) > 0

panels.title: Concurrent inserts ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the number of data ingestion requests that are being processed at the same time, where:
* `max` - the maximum number of requests that can be processed in parallel;
* `current` - the number of requests currently being processed.

If `current` frequently reaches `max`, VictoriaMetrics likely doesn't have enough resources to keep up with the ingestion rate. Add more CPU (see CPU usage) or faster disks (see disk read/write panels in the Resource Usage row).

The limit can be adjusted with the `-maxConcurrentInserts` command-line flag, but this isn't recommended in general, since it may increase memory usage.

panels.title: Pending datapoints
panels.description: How many data points are in RAM queue waiting to be written into storage. The number of pending data points should be in the range from 0 to `5*<ingestion_rate>`, since VictoriaMetrics pushes pending data to persistent storage every 5 seconds. The index datapoints value in general is much lower

panels.title: Active merges ($instance)
panels.description: The number of on-going merges in storage nodes.  It is expected to have high numbers for `storage/small` metric.

panels.title: Merge speed
panels.description: The number of rows merged per second by storage nodes.

panels.title: Disk space usage %  ($instance)
panels.description: Shows the percentage of used disk space. It is recommended to have at least 20% of free disk space for the best performance.

queries.query:
max(
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance) /
    (
        sum(vm_free_disk_space_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}-vm_free_disk_space_limit_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance) +
        sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance)
    ) 
)

min(
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance) /
    (
        sum(vm_free_disk_space_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}-vm_free_disk_space_limit_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance) +
        sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance)
    ) 
)

quantile(0.5,
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance) /
    (
        sum(vm_free_disk_space_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}-vm_free_disk_space_limit_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance) +
        sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance)
    ) 
)

panels.title: LSM parts max by type ($instance)
panels.description:
The max number of data parts of LSM tree across all storage nodes in the last [partition](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#storage).
Increase in number of parts (the hard limit is 512) is an evidence of slow merge performance - check the resource utilization.
* `indexdb` - inverted index
* `storage/small` - recently added parts of data ingested into storage (hot data)
* `storage/big` -  small parts gradually merged into bigger parts (cold data)

panels.title: Disk space usage % by type  ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the percentage of used disk space by type: datapoints or indexdb. Normally, indexdb takes much less space comparing to datapoints. But with high [churn rate](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/faq/#what-is-high-churn-rate) the size of the indexdb could grow significantly.

The sum of the % can be > 100% since panel shows max % per-job and per-instance. It means different instance can have different ratio between datapoints and indexdb size.

queries.query:
max(
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type=~"indexdb.*"}) by(job, instance)
    / 
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance)
)

max(
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type!~"indexdb.*"}) by(job, instance)
    / 
    sum(vm_data_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by(job, instance)
)

panels.description: Shows amount of on-disk space occupied by data points and the remaining disk space at `-storageDataPath`. Calculation accounts for -storage.minFreeDiskSpaceBytes

panels.title: Datapoints
panels.description: Shows how many datapoints are in the storage and what is average disk usage per datapoint.

/ sum(vm_rows{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", type!~"indexdb.*"}) by (job)

panels.title: Datapoints read per series
panels.description: 99th percentile of number of [data samples](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#raw-samples) read per queried series.

panels.title: Concurrent inserts ($instance)
panels.description:
Shows the number of data ingestion requests that are being processed at the same time, where:
* `max` - the maximum number of requests that can be processed in parallel;
* `current` - the number of requests currently being processed.

If `current` frequently reaches `max`, VictoriaMetrics likely doesn't have enough resources to keep up with the ingestion rate. Add more CPU (see CPU usage) or faster disks (see disk read/write panels in the Resource Usage row).

The limit can be adjusted with the `-maxConcurrentInserts` command-line flag, but this isn't recommended in general, since it may increase memory usage.

panels.title: Datapoints scanned per query
panels.description:
99th percentile of number of [data samples](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#raw-samples) scanner per query.

This number can exceed number of RowsReadPerQuery if `step` query arg passed to [/api/v1/query_range](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/querying/api/#range-queries) is smaller than the lookbehind window set in square brackets of [rollup function](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/metricsql/#rollup-functions). For example, if `increase(some_metric[1h])` is executed with the `step=5m`, then the same [data samples](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#raw-samples) on a hour time range are scanned `1h/5m=12` times. See [this article](https://valyala.medium.com/how-to-optimize-promql-and-metricsql-queries-85a1b75bf986) for details.

panels.title: Series read per query
panels.description: 99th percentile of number of series read per query.

panels.title: Datapoints read per query
panels.description: 99th percentile of number of [data samples](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/keyconcepts/#raw-samples) read per query.

panels.title: Number of snapshots
panels.description:
Shows number of existing [snapshots](https://docs.victoriametrics.com/victoriametrics/single-server-victoriametrics/#how-to-work-with-snapshots).

Recently made snapshots do not occupy disk space. But with time, as snapshots become older, they start to occupy more and more disk space.

It is recommended deleting old snapshots when they are no longer needed to free up disk space.

panels.content: Drilldown row is used by other panels on the dashboard to show more detailed metrics per-instance, or a single instance in cases like memory breakdown.

panels.description:
Major page faults occur when required data is not in physical memory and must be loaded from disk (storage or swap). It usually happens with:
- insufficient physical memory

It may cause significant performance slowdown if sustained high.

panels.title: Memory usage breakdown
panels.description:
This panel breaks down memory usage by type. It’s intended for inspecting a single instance.

How to use:
- Start from the high-level RSS panel.
- Identify an instance with unexpected or abnormal memory growth.
- Filter to that instance to inspect the detailed breakdown.

Interpretation
- A steadily rising Go Heap usually indicates a memory leak. Collect pprof memory profile.
- A growing Go Stack commonly points to a goroutine leak.

queries.query:
# go other
max(
    go_memstats_gc_sys_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} +
    go_memstats_mspan_sys_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} +
    go_memstats_other_sys_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} +
    go_memstats_mcache_sys_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}
)

# vm cache
max(sum(vm_cache_size_bytes{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}) by (job, instance))

The application's performance will significantly degrade when memory usage is close to 100%.

panels.title: Logging rate
panels.description: Shows the rate of logging the messages by their level. Unexpected spike in rate is a good reason to check logs.

queries.query: sum(rate(vm_log_messages_total{job=~"$job",instance=~"$instance", level!="info"}[$__rate_interval])) by (job, instance, level, app_version, location) > 0
